operative_clauses.judgment_reason: The single operative clause (the amendment of Instructions section XV-4 and Consular Regulations section 451 with the prohibition on accepting presents from foreign governments) ended on 1940-04-18, when Executive Order 8396 expressly revoked Executive Order 7577 of March 19, 1937 without condition. The date is the signing date of Executive Order 8396; that order states no separate effective date and was filed on April 19 and published on April 20, 1940. The held text shows no earlier ending: the order has no own end, and no earlier instrument that names it was found. The amending command was performed on issue, and the express revocation is the event that ended the order itself.

Executive  O rder
AMENDING THE INSTRUCTIONS TO DIPLOMATIC OFFICERS AND THE 
CONSULAR REGULATIONS
B y virtue o f and pursuant to thé authority vested in me  
by section 1752 of the Revised Statutes (U . S . C ., title 22,  
sec. 1 32), it is ordered th at section X V -4  o f the Instructions 
to Diplom atic Officers and section 451 of the Consular Regu­
lations be, and they are hereby, amended to read as follow s: *
“ Presents and testimonials. — No diplomatic or consular  
officer shall ask or accept for himself or any other per­
son, any present, em olument, office, or title of any kind  
from  any king, prince, or foreign state. (U . S. Const.,  
A rt. I, sec. 9, el. 8, U . S . C ., title 22, § 126.) Any present,  
decoration, order, or testim onial in acknowledgment of  
services rendered to th e citizens or governments  
of foreign states, or other thing, which shall be con - j 
ferred on or presented by any foreign government to  
any officer of the United States, shall be tendered through  
the Departm ent of State, and not to the individual in  
person, but such present, decoration, or other thing shall  
not be delivered by the Departm ent of State unless so  
authorized by act of Congress. (5 U . S. C ., § 115.)
“ Thorough consideration was given by the Committee  
on Foreign Affairs of the House o f Representatives in  
1934 to  the question whether the Congress should consent  
to the acceptance of presents, decorations, orders, medals,  
testim onials, or other things. I t resulted in  the enact­
m ent o f the join t resolution approved June 27, 1934 (48  
S ta t. 1267 ), which authorized only certain retired offi­
cers and employees therein nam ed to accept such decora­
tions, orders, m edals, or presents as had been tendered  
to them  by foreign governments. Hence it appears to be  
the settled policy of the Congress to decline to authorize  
the acceptance by civilian officers of the Government in  
active service of presents, decorations, medals, orders,  
testim onials, or other things, when presented to or con­
ferred on such officers by any king, prince, or foreign  
state. Furthermore, it  is contrary to the policy of the  
Governm ent to tender or to award presents, decorations,  
m edals, orders, testim onials, or other things to re p re -.  
sentatives of foreign governments. In  view of the atti­
tude of the Congress and the policy of the Government,  
Am erican diplom atic and consular officers are hereby  
prohibited  from  accepting in any circum stances  any  
present, decoration, m edal, order, testim onial, or other 
thing th at m ay be tendered to them by any foreign king,  
prince, or foreign state.”

research_rationale:
I read the complete held Federal Register original of Executive Order 7577 (2 FR 671, March 24, 1937; signed March 19, 1937). It is one order that amends section XV-4 of the Instructions to Diplomatic Officers and section 451 of the Consular Regulations to read as a new text on presents and testimonials, and that text prohibits diplomatic and consular officers from accepting any present, decoration, medal, order or testimonial from a foreign king, prince or state. It has no duration, condition, report or savings language. I read the complete held Federal Register text of Executive Order 8396 (5 FR 1461, April 20, 1940; signed April 18, 1940). Under its heading revoking executive orders, it states that the listed executive orders are revoked, and the list includes Executive Order No. 7577 dated March 19, 1937, with no condition, exception or deferred effective date. That express revocation is the first end of the order. I read the coverage notes of the three machine searches before selecting them: the U.S. Code search (edition through 2026-10-09, so laws enacted in the last five days before the 2026-10-14 cutoff are not reflected) and the eCFR search (as of 2026-10-14) found no citation of this order, and the Federal Register disposition-note search found the revocation by Executive Order 8396 and a catalog note that is blank about its effect, which the held revocation text supplies. No held instrument restores or revives Executive Order 7577 after the revocation. Original not an original grade issue: the Federal Register text layer is machine extracted and was checked only as text; the page images were not inspected.
Member checks: {"earlier_end_check":"The order has no end date, condition, report deadline or sunset in its own words; the three machine own-terms hits are sentences inside the quoted regulation text about gifts from foreign governments, not duration terms. The only held later instrument that names this order is Executive Order 8396, which revokes it; the status-history catalog lists only that revocation, and its note on the order is blank about effect, so the revocation text itself is the basis. A search of the held order-text folders by number, with OCR-tolerant patterns, found no earlier instrument that names, amends or suspends Executive Order 7577. The amending command was performed when the order was issued; the revocation ends the order itself, and no held source shows an earlier ending.","independent_command_check":"The only command is the amendment of the two regulation texts, which took effect when the order was issued. The order contains no report, delegation, appropriation or standing authority apart from that text. The prohibition in the prescribed text rests on the Constitution (Article I, section 9, clause 8) and on statutes that the text cites; those sources are independent of Executive Order 7577 and are not its commands. After the express revocation no command of Executive Order 7577 remains.","savings_check":"Executive Order 8396 contains no saving or exception clause for Executive Order 7577. The constitutional and statutory sources cited inside the amended text continue on their own authority and are not residuals of this order. No held source describes a right, appointment or proceeding that survived the revocation.","scope_check":"The revocation names Executive Order 7577 as a whole, with no partial limiter, no deferred effective date and no exception. The order has one operative clause (the amending command and the text it prescribes), and the inventory covers it from the heading to the end of the prescribed text; the machine note that segmentation is only a lead was resolved by reading the whole order. The end date is the signing date of Executive Order 8396, April 18, 1940, because the revoking order has no effective-date wording; it was filed April 19 and published April 20, 1940, which are later dates and are not used. If revocation were read as effective on filing or publication, the end would move by one or two days."}

savings_residuals.reason: Executive Order 8396 revokes Executive Order 7577 with no saving clause, exception or description of any accrued right or pending matter. The constitutional and statutory provisions that the amended text itself cites continue on their own authority and are not residual commands of Executive Order 7577. Bounded searches of the U.S. Code, the eCFR and the Federal Register disposition notes located no surviving command of this order.

operative_clauses.judgment_reason: The single clause (the reservation of the Sitka, Alaska lands for the Coast and Geodetic Survey as a magnetic and seismological observatory site) ended on 1941-08-16, when paragraph 1 of Executive Order 8854 revoked Executive Order 8168 of June 14, 1939 without condition. The date is the signing date of Executive Order 8854, which states no separate effective date and was filed on August 18 and published on August 20, 1941. Paragraph 2 of Executive Order 8854 separately reserves the same lands again, which is a new command and not a continuation of this clause. The held text shows no earlier ending.

research_rationale:
I read the complete held Federal Register original of Executive Order 8168 (4 FR 2415, June 16, 1939; signed June 14, 1939). After recitals that the Department of Agriculture no longer needed and had abandoned its Sitka, Alaska experiment-station lands, a single operative sentence revokes the Executive order of August 12, 1898 and reserves the lands for the Coast and Geodetic Survey of the Department of Commerce as a magnetic and seismological observatory site. It has no duration, condition or savings language. I read the complete held Federal Register text of Executive Order 8854 (6 FR 4181, August 20, 1941; signed August 16, 1941), titled as revoking Executive Order 8168. The Federal Register text layer renders the order number in the quotation as 81681 (a footnote mark run into the number); the actual checker reads that as a different order and reports a mechanical order-exists failure, which is an extraction artifact. An American Presidency Project transcription of the same order is held and agrees in substance, but an official copy is held, so the transcription may not be used as the quoted source. Paragraph 1 orders that Executive Order No. 8168 of June 14, 1939, is revoked, with no condition or exception. Paragraph 2 separately withdraws the lands contained in the 8168 reservation and an adjoining tract for the same Survey use under the President's own authority. Paragraph 2 is a new reservation made by Executive Order 8854, not a continuation of Executive Order 8168, so the whole of Executive Order 8168 ended on August 16, 1941. I read the coverage notes of the three machine searches before selecting them: the U.S. Code search (through 2026-10-09) and the eCFR search (as of 2026-10-14) found no citation of this order, and the Federal Register disposition-note search found only the revocation by Executive Order 8854 (two catalog entries for the same event). The Federal Register text layer is machine extracted and was checked only as text; the page images were not inspected.

The only later instrument found in the held order-text folders by number that names it is Executive Order 8854; the held texts labelled Executive Orders 8853, 8855 and 8856 reproduce the same Federal Register pages as Executive Order 8854 and are not separate orders. The status-history catalog lists only the Executive Order 8854 revocation. A prior provisional status proposal in the repository reached the same reading and is not relied on as a source. No earlier ending, amendment or suspension was found.","independent_command_check":"Executive Order 8168 has one command, the reservation of the Sitka lands for the Coast and Geodetic Survey; the revocation of the 1898 order that it recites in the same sentence was performed on issue. Paragraph 2 of Executive Order 8854 reserves the same lands again on its own authority; that is a separate command of a later order and does not keep any command of Executive Order 8168 alive.","savings_check":"Executive Order 8854 has no saving clause for Executive Order 8168. The lands remain reserved for the Survey, but under the new reservation in paragraph 2 of Executive Order 8854, which is recorded as a continuing independent command and not as a residual of Executive Order 8168.","scope_check":"Paragraph 1 of Executive Order 8854 revokes the whole of Executive Order 8168, with no partial limiter, deferred effective date or exception. The inventory is one clause covering the recitals and the operative sentence, because machine segmentation found no finer boundary; I confirmed it covers the whole order text from the heading to the end of the operative sentence. The end date is the signing date of Executive Order 8854, August 16, 1941, because it has no effective-date wording; it was filed August 18 and published August 20, 1941, which are later dates and are not used."}

savings_residuals.reason: Paragraph 2 of Executive Order 8854 independently withdraws and reserves the lands that Executive Order 8168 had reserved, together with an adjoining tract, for the Coast and Geodetic Survey. That later reservation is a separate command of Executive Order 8854 and continues independently of the ended Executive Order 8168. No saving clause preserves any provision of Executive Order 8168 itself.

as President of the United States, it is 
hereby ordered that there be exempted 
from the operation of Executive Order 
No. 6746 of June 21, 1934, prescribing a 
salary schedule for certain positions not 
subject to the Classification Act as 
amended, the positions of consultants, 
experts, specialists, attorneys, and other 
similar positions, the incumbents of 
which are intermittently employed on a
per diem  basis or employed on an annual 
basis at amounts representing the value 
of part-time service required, and who 
are or have been paid from the public 
works or other emergency funds admin­
istered by the Secretary of the Interior 
or by the Federal Works Administrator 
through the Commissioner of Public 
Works, available during the fiscal year 
1942.

A vessel may expect supervision of its 
movements within the Manila Bay De­
fensive Sea Area, either through surface 
craft or aircraft. Such controlling sur­
face craft and aircraft will be identified 
by a prominent display of the Union 
Jack.
These regulations are subject to ampli­
fication by the local United States Naval 
authority as necessary to meet local 
circumstances and conditions.
When a United States Maritime Con­
trol Area is established adjacent to or 
abutting upon the above-established de­
fensive sea area, it shall be assumed that 
permission to enter, and other instruc­
tions issued by proper authority, shall 
apply to any one continuous passage 
through or within both areas.
Any master of a vessel or other person 
within the Manila Bay Defensive Sea 
Area who shall disregard these regula­
tions, or shall fail to obey an order of 
United States Naval authority to stop or 
heave to, or shall perform any act threat­
ening the efficiency of mine or other 
defenses or the safety of navigation, or 
shall take any action inimical to the 
interests of the United States, may be 
detained therein by force of arms and 
shall be liable to attack by United States 
armed forces, and liable to prosecution 
as provided for in section 44 of the 
Criminal Code, as amended (U.S.C., title 
18, sec. 96).
All United States Government authori­
ties shall place at the disposal of the 
Naval authorities their facilities for aid­
ing in the enforcement of these regula­
tions.
The Secretary of the Navy will be 
charged with the publication and en­
forcement of these regulations.
